transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess I'm here because things at the store are getting... complicated. I supervise the retail floor, so I have to explain things to the team, right? Like the inventory numbers, or mapping out the weekend schedule. But lately, when I try to do that, my words just start jumping all over the place. 

I'll be talking about the freight trucks coming in, and then suddenly I'm talking about Thursdays. Thursday is usually when we fire up the church grill—well, not at the store, at my parish. We got this new charcoal smoker last month, beautiful stainless steel, really holds the heat well if you're doing a brisket. My neighbor actually brought his famous coleslaw to the last one, he uses a little bit of apple cider vinegar in it, which makes a huge difference. 

But, um... right, the store. I'll be trying to explain the schedule, and suddenly I'm going on about the grill, or my boss's tone of voice on the phone, and the trucks... all mixed together. And the staff, they just stare at me. They look at me like they absolutely can't follow a single thing I'm saying.
When you're talking and your thoughts jump around like that, are you aware that you're doing it while it's happening, or do you only notice afterward when people give you that confused look?

Well, I... I think I only really notice when they start giving me that look, you know? Like I'm speaking a different language. It's frustrating because I feel like I'm making perfect sense in the moment. Just like when I was trying to explain to my son how to change the oil in his car. He's got this old Honda Civic, a '98, I think. Great little car, runs forever if you treat it right. You just have to make sure you don't over-tighten the oil filter, otherwise it's a nightmare to get off the next time. I always tell him, hand-tighten it, then maybe a quarter turn with the wrench. Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the store. Yeah, I don't really realize I'm doing it until they stare at me.
When you're thinking to yourself—not talking out loud, just in your head—do your thoughts jump around the same way, or does that mainly happen when you're trying to speak to other people?

In my head? No, in my head it all lines up perfectly. It's really just when I open my mouth. Like I was saying a minute ago, I'll be trying to lay out the inventory numbers or the weekend schedule for the floor staff, and the words just start jumping from the freight trucks to Thursdays, to the church grill, to my boss’s tone of voice. 

And speaking of his tone, he called yesterday, and he has this real nasally way of talking. He grew up upstate, near Syracuse, I think. I went to Syracuse once back in '88 for a regional meeting. The snow up there is unbelievable. It came down so hard one night we couldn't even see the streetlamps, just these big white mounds where the cars were supposed to be parked. My buddy had this maroon Ford Taurus, and we had to dig it out with a plastic dustpan from the hotel lobby because all the snow shovels were sold out at the local hardware store. Took us half the morning just to clear the windshield. 

But, um... yeah, so in my head, the thoughts are fine. It's just when I try to get them out loud that it all gets jumbled up, and they just stare at me like they can't follow a single thing I'm saying.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with expressive language disorder characterized by significant difficulty organizing and sequencing speech output despite intact internal thought processes. Speech is marked by tangential, disorganized verbal output with frequent topic shifts that impair communication effectiveness in occupational and social contexts. Internal cognition remains organized, indicating the disorder is specific to speech production/expression rather than a global cognitive or thought disorder. Onset and chronicity suggest a persistent language-based difficulty.
